newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Zairean opposition to defy ban and march.
newsitem.headline: Zairean opposition to defy ban and march.

text.p: The main political opposition in Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo has called a protest march for Wednesday in defiance of a ban, one day before he takes office as president.
Opposition militants, banned from political activity, told a news conference on Tuesday they would take to the streets to demand the departure of foreign troops and proper political dialogue.

Kabila, who proclaimed himself president on May 17 as his rebels entered the capital Kinshasa, left the city on Tuesday for the southern mining centre of Lubumbashi, officials said, adding that he would return in time for Thursday's inauguration.
Witnesses, meanwhile, reported sustained gunfire near a military camp in central Kinshasa late on Tuesday. The cause was not immediately clear.
"We are restoring order, we know that there are enemies and that demonstrations boost supporters of the former regime," Information Minister Raphael Ghenda told Reuters late on Tuesday.
"People say (we) must be given time to show what (we) can do and if they are not happy then of course (there can be) demonstrations," he said.
State radio and television said Kabila would take office in a ceremony at the People's Palace parliament building and that the inauguration would be his "first official outing".
Officials declined to say why he had gone to Lubumbashi.
Opposition activists promised protests this week and next.

"Despite the ban, there will be a democratic march tomorrow," said Jean-Marie Vianney Kabukanye, national secretary of the youth wing of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi.

"We have not changed Mobutu to replace him with another Mobutu. The man has changed but not the policies," Vianney told Reuters in the opposition stronghold of Limete. Kabila's forces did not try to prevent him giving a news conference.
The statement announcing the ban said anyone infringing it would be considered an "enemy of the liberation of the people". It said the ban would apply until further notice.
Opposition activists marched in Kinshasa on Friday and Saturday. Kabila forces fired in the air and took away some protesters. Government officials said they were later released.
Tshisekedi, citing a 1992 vote at a national conference in what was then Zaire, has doggedly insisted over the years that constitutionally he is prime minister.
Kabila's ministers accuse Tshisekedi of misleading the people to feed his own ambition.
Tshisekedi aides say Kabila has deployed troops from Rwanda and other neighbouring countries in the capital and accuse him of seeking to return to a one-party state.
"Foreign troops must leave as soon as possible or risk appearing like occupation troops," Vianney said.
Kabila aides say he plans to increase the government from 13 to 20 ministers but without appointing a prime minister.
